title: Complex Eigenvalues and Rotation
intro: Some matrices keep no direction at all: they turn every vector. Their eigenvalues are complex numbers, and the complex numbers are not a nuisance here but the answer, because a complex eigenvalue is a statement about turning and scaling at once. This page works it out for rotations, then for any matrix with a complex pair, and then in three dimensions.

blocks.text: A matrix with no real eigenvector
Rotate the plane by an angle $\theta$ anticlockwise. The rotation matrix is

Its columns are where $e_1 = (1, 0)$ and $e_2 = (0, 1)$ land: $e_1$ goes to $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ and $e_2$ goes to $(-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$. Every vector turns through $\theta$ and keeps its length. For $\theta = 30°$ no vector stays on its own line, so there is no real eigenvector: an eigenvector would have to stay put, and nothing does. (Two exceptions: $\theta = 0$ is the identity, and $\theta = 180°$ turns every vector onto the opposite side of its own line, so every vector is an eigenvector with $\lambda = -1$.)

Does the characteristic polynomial, from Finding Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/math/eigenvalues/finding-eigenvalues), agree? The trace is $2\cos\theta$ and the determinant is $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$, so

The quantity under the root, $4\cos^2\theta - 4 = -4\sin^2\theta$, is negative unless $\sin\theta = 0$, so for most angles the roots are not real. Here $j$ is the square root of $-1$. (Mathematicians and physicists write $i$; engineers write $j$ because $i$ means current, and this topic follows the other engineering pages on this site.) The roots are $\cos\theta \pm j\sin\theta$, which is $e^{\pm j\theta}$ by Euler's formula: two points on the unit circle in the complex plane, at angles $+\theta$ and $-\theta$. The matrix has no scaling effect (both roots have $|\lambda| = 1$), and the angle of $\lambda$ is the angle of the rotation. For $\theta = 30°$: $\lambda = 0.866 \pm 0.5j$, which is what the viewer prints for the rotation preset.
Complex eigenvalues come in pairs

This is not special to rotations. If $A$ has only real entries then its characteristic polynomial has real coefficients. Take the complex conjugate of the equation $p(\lambda) = 0$ and, since conjugating a sum or product does the same to each piece and real coefficients do not change, $p(\bar\lambda) = 0$ too. So non-real roots arrive in pairs $a \pm bj$, and a real $2 \times 2$ matrix has either two real eigenvalues or one conjugate pair. The same works for the eigenvectors: conjugate $Av = \lambda v$, and since $A$ is real, $A\bar v = \bar\lambda \bar v$. The conjugate eigenvalue has the conjugate eigenvector. The discriminant, $\text{trace}^2 - 4\det$, being negative is the test.
The eigenvector, worked

Complex eigenvalues have complex eigenvectors, found by the same method as before. Take $\theta = 90°$, $R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, with $\lambda = j$. Then $A - \lambda I = \begin{pmatrix} -j & -1 \\ 1 & -j \end{pmatrix}$ and we need $(A - jI)v = 0$. The first row says $-j v_1 - v_2 = 0$, so $v_2 = -j v_1$, and with $v_1 = 1$ the eigenvector is $v = (1, -j)$. The second row agrees: $v_1 - j v_2 = 1 - j(-j) = 1 - 1 = 0$. Check directly: $R v = (0 \cdot 1 + (-1)(-j),\ 1 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot (-j)) = (j, 1)$, and $jv = (j, -j^2) = (j, 1)$. Equal, so $Rv = jv$.

The same vector $(1, -j)$ works for any $\theta$ with $\lambda = e^{j\theta}$, and $(1, j)$ goes with $e^{-j\theta}$: a rotation has the same two complex eigenvectors whatever the angle. Check for general $\theta$: $R(1, -j) = (\cos\theta + j\sin\theta,\ \sin\theta - j\cos\theta)$, and the second entry equals $-j(\cos\theta + j\sin\theta)$, so the whole vector is $(\cos\theta + j\sin\theta)\,(1, -j)$. It is a complex multiple of $(1, -j)$ with multiplier $e^{j\theta}$.
What does a vector with an imaginary part mean on a real plane? On its own, nothing you can draw. The real meaning is in the pair of real vectors it contains, which the next section extracts.
What a ± bj means: scale and turn

Write $\lambda = a + bj$ in polar form: $r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ is its size and $\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(b, a)$ is its angle, so $\lambda = r e^{j\theta}$. Multiplying a complex number by $\lambda$ scales it by $r$ and rotates it by $\theta$. The claim is that the matrix does the same thing to the real plane, in a suitable set of axes. The matrix that scales by $r$ and rotates by $\theta$ is

Here is why every real $2 \times 2$ matrix with eigenvalue $a + bj$ is this matrix in disguise. Let $v = u + jw$ be an eigenvector, with $u$ and $w$ its real and imaginary parts (both real vectors). Then $Av = \lambda v$ reads

blocks.tex: A(u + jw) = (a + bj)(u + jw) = (au - bw) + j(bu + aw)

blocks.text: Since $A$ is real, $Au$ and $Aw$ are real, so matching real and imaginary parts gives $Au = au - bw$ and $Aw = bu + aw$. In words: $A$ sends the real vector $u$ to a mix of $u$ and $w$, and sends $w$ to another mix of the same two. The plane spanned by $u$ and $w$ (they are independent when $b \ne 0$) is mapped into itself, and in the basis $w, u$ the matrix of $A$ is read off from those two equations: $Aw = a w + b u$ is the first column $(a, b)$ and $Au = -b w + a u$ is the second column $(-b, a)$. So, with $P$ having $w$ and $u$ as its columns,

blocks.tex: A = P \begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix} P^{-1}, \qquad P = \begin{pmatrix} w & u \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \operatorname{Im} v & \operatorname{Re} v \end{pmatrix}

blocks.text: The order of the columns matters. With $P = (\operatorname{Re} v,\ \operatorname{Im} v)$ you get $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ -b & a \end{pmatrix}$ instead, a rotation the other way; both are correct and they differ only by the choice of which basis vector comes first. This is the real analogue of diagonalisation in Diagonalisation and Powers (#/math/eigenvalues/diagonalisation): we cannot reach a diagonal matrix with real numbers, but we can reach a scaled rotation.
A full example

Take $A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. The trace is 4 and the determinant is $3 + 2 = 5$, so $\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 5 = 0$ and $\lambda = (4 \pm \sqrt{16 - 20})/2 = 2 \pm j$. Here $a = 2$ and $b = 1$: the size is $r = \sqrt{5} = 2.236$ and the angle is $\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(1, 2) = 26.57°$.

For the eigenvector of $\lambda = 2 + j$: $A - \lambda I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - j & -2 \\ 1 & -1 - j \end{pmatrix}$. The second row says $v_1 = (1 + j)\, v_2$, so take $v_2 = 1$ and $v = (1 + j, 1)$. Check against the first row: $(1 - j)(1 + j) - 2 = 1 - j^2 - 2 = 0$. Check directly: $Av = (3 + 3j - 2,\ 1 + j + 1) = (1 + 3j,\ 2 + j)$, and $\lambda v = ((2 + j)(1 + j),\ 2 + j) = (2 + 2j + j + j^2,\ 2 + j) = (1 + 3j,\ 2 + j)$. Equal.

Split $v = (1 + j, 1) = (1, 1) + j\,(1, 0)$, so $u = (1, 1)$ and $w = (1, 0)$. Then $P = \begin{pmatrix} w & u \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $P^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Multiply: $AP$ has columns $Aw = (3, 1)$ and $Au = (1, 2)$, so $AP = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, and $P^{-1}AP$ has rows $(3 - 1,\ 1 - 2) = (2, -1)$ and $(1, 2)$:

This is the promised form, with $a = 2$ and $b = 1$. In the right axes, $A$ turns by 26.57° and scales by 2.236. In the usual axes the picture is a tilted version of that: the unit circle becomes a tilted ellipse, because $P$ is not a rotation. The next viewer sets up this matrix with its sliders.

Rotation and scaling in the viewer

Three presets show the three kinds of complex pair, and the size $r = |\lambda|$ decides which. Because each of these matrices is itself of the form $r R_\theta$, it turns and scales every vector alike, and the dots of the powers show it.

items: $r = 1$, a pure rotation: the preset 'rotation by 30°' has $\lambda = 0.866 \pm 0.5j$. Powers of $A$ turn $v$ by 30° each time without changing its length, so $A^{12} = I$ and $A^6 = -I$ (a half turn).

$r > 1$, a spiral outwards: 'rotate and grow' $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has $\lambda = 1 \pm j$, $r = \sqrt{2} = 1.414$ and angle 45°. Eight steps make one full turn and multiply the length by $\sqrt{2}^{\,8} = 16$.

$r < 1$, a spiral inwards: 'spiral in' $\begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & -0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$ has $\lambda = 0.8 \pm 0.3j$, $r = \sqrt{0.73} = 0.854$ and angle 20.6°. A full turn takes $360/20.56 = 17.5$ steps, and each step multiplies the length by 0.854.

Rotation in three dimensions

A real $3 \times 3$ matrix has a cubic characteristic polynomial. A cubic with real coefficients goes from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ (or the reverse) as $\lambda$ runs along the real line, so it crosses zero somewhere: there is always a real eigenvalue. The other two roots are either real or a conjugate pair. A real $3 \times 3$ matrix therefore cannot turn every line through the origin off itself: at least one line is kept (stretched, shrunk or flipped, but not turned). For a rotation that kept line is the axis, which is why a turning object in space always has one.

A rotation of space by $\theta$ about an axis $n$ has the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1$ with eigenvector $n$ (the axis is untouched), and the plane perpendicular to the axis is turned by $\theta$, which gives the pair $e^{\pm j\theta}$. The trace is the sum of the eigenvalues,

so given any rotation matrix you can find its angle from the trace alone: $\cos\theta = (\operatorname{tr} R - 1)/2$. And its axis is the eigenvector for $\lambda = 1$. (The trace cannot tell whether the turn is clockwise or anticlockwise; that depends on which way along the axis you look.) The preset 'rotation by 60° about the z-axis' has trace $0.5 + 0.5 + 1 = 2 = 1 + 2\cos 60°$.

blocks.text: The numbers panel reads $\lambda = 1$ along $(0, 0, 1)$, and $\lambda = 0.5 \pm 0.866j$ with $|\lambda| = 1$ and angle 60°, and 'not symmetric'. The one dashed line is the z-axis and the amber disc is the plane being turned, the xy-plane. Press Next step ▶ to step 5: 'only one real direction survives'. Set Powers shown, k, to 6: six turns of 60° bring $v$ back to where it began, so the readout's $A^6v$ equals $v$.

A less obvious rotation is the cyclic shift $(x, y, z) \mapsto (z, x, y)$, with matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. It is a permutation, so it does not obviously rotate anything. Its trace is 0, so $\cos\theta = (0 - 1)/2 = -1/2$ and $\theta = 120°$. The axis: $(1, 1, 1)$ goes to $(1, 1, 1)$, so it is the eigenvector with $\lambda = 1$. The shift is a one-third turn about the body diagonal, and doing it three times gives the identity, $A^3 = I$. The lessons

items: A real matrix with no real eigenvalue turns every vector; its eigenvalues are a conjugate pair $a \pm bj$.

The size $r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ is the scale factor per step and the angle $\operatorname{atan2}(b, a)$ is the turn per step. Powers spiral in if $r < 1$, circle if $r = 1$ and spiral out if $r > 1$. This is why $|\lambda| < 1$ is the stability test for repeated multiplication (compare the unit circle in The Z-Transform (#/math/z-transform)) and why Re $\lambda < 0$ is the test for differential equations (The Laplace Transform (#/math/laplace-transform)); Eigenvalues in Practice (#/math/eigenvalues/applications) develops both.

In the basis $\operatorname{Im} v$, $\operatorname{Re} v$ (in that order) made from the eigenvector $v$ of $a + bj$, the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}$; in the order $\operatorname{Re} v$, $\operatorname{Im} v$ it is $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ -b & a \end{pmatrix}$.
In 3D a real matrix always has a real eigenvalue; for a rotation it is 1, its eigenvector is the axis, and $\operatorname{tr} = 1 + 2\cos\theta$.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Read off the turn
blocks.text: Find the eigenvalues of $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and say what $A$ does to a vector.
solution: In the form $a + bj$ this is $a = 0$, $b = 2$: size $r = 2$ and angle $\operatorname{atan2}(2, 0) = 90°$. The matrix is already $\begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}$ with $a = 0$, $b = 2$. It turns every vector by 90° and doubles its length. Check: $A(1, 0) = (0, 2)$.
Twice over, $A^2 = -4I$: a half turn with length times 4.

blocks.title: Spiral out or in?
blocks.text: For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ find the eigenvalues, the size and the angle, and say what happens to the length of $A^k v$ as $k$ grows. By how much does it grow in 8 steps?
solution: Trace 2 and determinant $0 + 2 = 2$. Then $\lambda^2 - 2\lambda + 2 = 0$ and $\lambda = (2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 8})/2 = 1 \pm j$.

Size $r = \sqrt{1 + 1} = \sqrt{2} = 1.414$, angle $\operatorname{atan2}(1, 1) = 45°$. Since $r > 1$, vectors spiral outwards. This matrix is not of the form $\begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}$, so a given vector's length does not grow by exactly $\sqrt{2}$ at each step; it rises and falls around that trend, because the circle becomes a tilted ellipse.

Over eight steps the eigenvalues become $(1 \pm j)^8 = (\sqrt{2})^8 e^{\pm j 360°} = 16$, both the same, and a diagonalisable matrix with a single eigenvalue 16 is $16I$. So $A^8 = 16I$ exactly: after eight steps every vector is back in its own direction, 16 times longer. This is the same $A^8$ as for the rotate-and-grow preset, which you can check there.
blocks.answer: $\lambda = 1 \pm j$, $r = \sqrt{2}$, 45°; it spirals outwards, with $A^8$ equal to $16I$.

blocks.title: Angle from the trace
blocks.text: A $3 \times 3$ rotation matrix has trace 2.5. Find the rotation angle. What is the trace for a half turn?
solution: For a half turn, $\theta = 180°$, $\cos\theta = -1$ and the trace is $1 - 2 = -1$. The eigenvalues are then $1, -1, -1$.
blocks.answer: $\theta = 41.41°$; the trace of a half turn is $-1$.

blocks.title: How long to fade?
blocks.text: The 'spiral in' matrix has $r = 0.854$ and angle 20.6°. How many steps until a vector's length has dropped below one tenth, and how many turns has it made by then?
solution: Each step turns 20.56°, so 15 steps turn $15 \times 20.56° = 308°$, about 0.86 of a full turn.
blocks.answer: 15 steps, a little under one turn.
